title: Blade II
full_review:
Wesley Snipes reprises his role as a vampire chaser, this time to catch an uber-vampire who kills mortals and monsters alike in the gory -- and boring -- horror-action sequel "Blade II" (New Line).

The Blade (Snipes) character is a creation of Marv Wolfman and Gene Colan for Marvel Comics. Half man, half vampire, Blade (or Day Walker as his friends and enemies call him) has all the strength of a bloodsucker but none of the weaknesses. In this sequel, poorly directed by Guillermo del Toro, Blade teams up with the very creatures he hates to fight off an extra-powerful vampire named Nomak (Luke Goss) who feeds off human blood just as easily as he does Dracula's. And each time Nomak bites, he leaves behind a virus in his victim's body that transforms them into beasts like himself.

This ridiculous story line quickly develops into a tedious bloodfest where exploding vampires disintegrate into fiery ashes but not before various body parts are flung in every direction and buckets of blood are splattered. (This trick is used over and over and over again.) Almost every second of the film is taken up with some sort of combat, gunplay or sword fight. But these fight sequences are so artificial, with every punch, kick and body blow precisely choreographed, that the characters might as well be doing a tango (albeit, a violent tango, not a romantic one).

The special effects range from creative (Nomak's lower lip splits to reveal a vicious wagging tongue and saber-like teeth) to staid (vampires flying through the air to deliver a powerful kick reminiscent of "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon"). And some of the action scenes give off a canned video game vibe, as if the viewer is suddenly watching an arcade game screen and not a movie screen.

Director del Toro is capable of much finer work, such as last year's ghost yarn "The Devil's Backbone," in which he created spooky atmospherics without succumbing to hokey special effects. But in this film, he seems to be just going along for the ride.

Snipes plays his part with ultra-seriousness, which is a mistake because a little wink to the audience could have gone a long way toward injecting some fun into the film. Instead, Snipes spouts absurd dialogue with a straight face as if he really is master of the universe. Kris Kristofferson is also back from the original movie, making little impact in his role as Blade's old-man sidekick.

"Blade II" is instantly forgettable. So much so, that audiences may wish to forget the film even as they watch.

Due to non-stop violence, excessively brutal and gruesome imagery and recurring rough language with some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
